Albuquerque returned home in July 1504 and was well received by King Manuel I. After he assisted with the creation of a strategy for the Portuguese efforts in the east, King Manuel entrusted him with the command of a squadron of five vessels in the fleet of sixteen sailing for India in early 1506, headed by [Tristão da Cunha](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trist%C3%A3o_da_Cunha "Tristão da Cunha").[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Afonso_de_Albuquerque#cite_note-Chisholm-8) The aim of the expedition was to conquer [Socotra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Socotra "Socotra") and build a fortress there, hoping to close the trade in the Red Sea.

Albuquerque went as "chief-captain for the [Coast of Arabia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arabian_Peninsula "Arabian Peninsula")", sailing under da Cunha's orders until reaching Mozambique.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Afonso_de_Albuquerque#cite_note-22) He carried a sealed letter with a secret mission ordered by the king: after fulfilling the first mission, he was to replace the first viceroy of India, [Francisco de Almeida](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Francisco_de_Almeida "Francisco de Almeida"), whose term ended two years later.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Afonso_de_Albuquerque#cite_note-Foundations-6) Before departing, he legitimized his son Brás ("Braz" in the old Portuguese spelling), born to a common Portuguese woman named Joana Vicente in 1500.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Afonso_de_Albuquerque#cite_note-23)

### First conquest of Socotra, Muscat and Ormuz, 1507

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Afonso_de_Albuquerque&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: First conquest of Socotra, Muscat and Ormuz, 1507")]

Main article: [Capture of Ormuz (1507)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capture_of_Ormuz_(1507) "Capture of Ormuz (1507)")

The fleet left Lisbon on 6 April 1506. Albuquerque piloted his ship himself, having lost his appointed pilot on departure. In [Mozambique Channel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Juan_de_Nova_Island "Juan de Nova Island"), they rescued Captain [João da Nova](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jo%C3%A3o_da_Nova "João da Nova"), who had encountered difficulties on his return from India; da Nova and his ship, the _[Flor de la mar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flor\_de\_la\_Mar "Flor de la Mar")_, joined da Cunha's fleet.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Afonso_de_Albuquerque#cite_note-Commentaries_of_the_Great_Afonso-24) From [Malindi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malindi "Malindi"), da Cunha sent envoys to [Ethiopia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ethiopia "Ethiopia"), which at the time was thought to be closer to India than it actually is, under the aegis of Albuquerque. After failing to reach Ethiopia, he managed to land the envoys in [Filuk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cape_Guardafui "Cape Guardafui").[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Afonso_de_Albuquerque#cite_note-Stones-25) After successful attacks on Arab cities on the East African coast, the expedition conquered the island of [Socotra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Socotra "Socotra") and built a fortress at Suq, hoping to establish a base to stop the Red Sea commerce to the Indian Ocean. However, Socotra was abandoned four years later, as it was eventually realised to be a poor location for a base.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Afonso_de_Albuquerque#cite_note-Foundations-6)

[![Image 9](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/e4/Portuguese_Castle_%28Hormuz%29.jpg/250px-Portuguese_Castle_%28Hormuz%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Portuguese_Castle_(Hormuz).jpg)

The [Fort of Our Lady of the Conception](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fort_of_Our_Lady_of_the_Conception_in_Hormoz_island "Fort of Our Lady of the Conception in Hormoz island"), [Hormuz Island](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hormuz_Island "Hormuz Island"), Iran

At Socotra, they parted ways: Tristão da Cunha sailed for India, where he would relieve the Portuguese [besieged at Cannanore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Cannanore_(1507) "Siege of Cannanore (1507)"), while Afonso took seven ships and 500 men to [Ormuz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ormuz "Ormuz") in the Persian Gulf, one of the chief eastern centers of commerce. On his way, he conquered the cities of Curiati (Kuryat), [Muscat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capture_of_Muscat_(1507) "Capture of Muscat (1507)") in July 1507, and [Khor Fakkan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Khor_Fakkan "Khor Fakkan"), accepting the submission of the cities of Kalhat and [Sohar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sohar "Sohar"). He arrived at [Hormuz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ormus "Ormus") on 25 September and soon [captured the city](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capture_of_Ormuz_(1507) "Capture of Ormuz (1507)"), which agreed to become a tributary state of the Portuguese king.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Afonso_de_Albuquerque#cite_note-26)

[![Image 10](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/09/Afonso_de_Albuquerque_Lisboa.jpg/250px-Afonso_de_Albuquerque_Lisboa.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Afonso_de_Albuquerque_Lisboa.jpg)

Statue of Afonso de Albuquerque, symbolically standing on a stack of weapons, referencing his reply in Hormuz

Ormuz was then a tributary state of [Shah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shah "Shah")[Ismail I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ismail_I "Ismail I") (r.1501–1524) of [Safavid Persia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Safavid_Iran "Safavid Iran"). In a famous episode, shortly after its conquest, Albuquerque was confronted by Persian envoys, who demanded the payment of the due tribute from him instead. He ordered them to be given a stock of cannonballs, arrows and weapons, retorting that "such was the currency struck in Portugal to pay the tribute demanded from the dominions of King Manuel".[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Afonso_de_Albuquerque#cite_note-27) According to Brás de Albuquerque, it was Shah Ismael who first addressed Albuquerque as "Lion of the seas".[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Afonso_de_Albuquerque#cite_note-Commentaries_of_the_Great_Afonso-24)

Afonso began building the [Fort of Our Lady of Victory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fort_of_Our_Lady_of_the_Conception_in_Hormoz_island "Fort of Our Lady of the Conception in Hormoz island") (later renamed Fort of Our Lady of the Conception)[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Afonso_de_Albuquerque#cite_note-28) on Hormuz Island, engaging his men of all ranks in the work.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Afonso_de_Albuquerque#cite_note-29) However, some of his officers, claiming that Afonso was exceeding his orders, revolted against the heavy work and climate and departed for India. With his fleet reduced to two ships and left without supplies, he was unable to maintain his position. In January 1508, he was forced to abandon Ormuz. He raided coastal villages to resupply the settlement of Socotra, returned to Ormuz, and then headed to India.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Afonso_de_Albuquerque#cite_note-30)

### Arrest at Cannanore, 1509

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Afonso_de_Albuquerque&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Arrest at Cannanore, 1509")]

Afonso arrived at [Cannanore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kannur "Kannur") on the [Malabar coast](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malabarian_Coast "Malabarian Coast") in December 1508, where he opened the sealed letter that he had received from the king before the viceroy, Dom Francisco de Almeida, which named him as governor to succeed Almeida.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Afonso_de_Albuquerque#cite_note-Foundations-6) The viceroy, supported by the officers who had abandoned Afonso at Ormuz, had a matching royal order but declined to yield. He protested that his term ended only in January and stated his intention to avenge his son's death by fighting the [Mamluk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mamluk_Sultanate_(Cairo) "Mamluk Sultanate (Cairo)") fleet of [Mirocem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mirocem "Mirocem"), refusing Afonso's offer to fight the Mamluk fleet himself. Afonso avoided confrontation, which could have led to civil war, and moved to [Kochi, India](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kochi,_India "Kochi, India"), to await further instruction from the king. Increasingly isolated, he wrote to [Diogo Lopes de Sequeira](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diogo_Lopes_de_Sequeira "Diogo Lopes de Sequeira"), who arrived in India with a new fleet, but was ignored as Sequeira joined Almeida. At the same time, Afonso refused approaches from opponents of Almeida who encouraged him to seize power.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Afonso_de_Albuquerque#cite_note-31)

On 3 February 1509, Almeida fought the naval [Battle of Diu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Diu "Battle of Diu") against a joint fleet of [Mamluks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burji_dynasty "Burji dynasty"), [Ottomans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ottoman_Empire "Ottoman Empire"), the [Zamorin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zamorin "Zamorin") of [Calicut](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kozhikode "Kozhikode"), and the [Sultan of Gujarat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mahmud_Begada "Mahmud Begada"). His victory was decisive: the Ottomans and Mamluks abandoned the Indian Ocean, easing the way for Portuguese rule there for the next century. In August, after a petition from Afonso's former officers with the support of Diogo Lopes de Sequeira claiming him unfit for governance, Afonso was sent in custody to [St. Angelo Fort](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Angelo_Fort "St. Angelo Fort") in [Cannanore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kannur_district "Kannur district").[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Afonso_de_Albuquerque#cite_note-32)[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Afonso_de_Albuquerque#cite_note-33) There he remained under what he considered as imprisonment.

## Governor of Portuguese India, 1509–1515

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Afonso_de_Albuquerque&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Governor of Portuguese India, 1509–1515")]

[![Image 11](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/bf/Afonso_de_Albuquerque_%28with_Santiago_cloak%29.jpg/250px-Afonso_de_Albuquerque_%28with_Santiago_cloak%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Afonso_de_Albuquerque_(with_Santiago_cloak).jpg)

Afonso de Albuquerque as Governor of India

Afonso was released after three months' confinement, on the arrival at Cannanore of the [Marshal of Portugal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marshal_of_Portugal "Marshal of Portugal")[Fernando Coutinho](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fernando_Coutinho?action=edit&redlink=1 "Fernando Coutinho (page does not exist)") with a large fleet sent by the king.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Afonso_de_Albuquerque#cite_note-Chisholm-8) Coutinho was the most important Portuguese noble to visit India up to that point. He brought an armada of fifteen ships and 3,000 men to defend Afonso's rights, and to take [Calicut](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kozhikode "Kozhikode").[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Afonso_de_Albuquerque#cite_note-34)

On 4 November 1509, Afonso became the second Governor of Portuguese India, a position he would hold until his death. Almeida set off to return to Portugal, but he was killed before he got there in a skirmish with the [Khoekhoe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Khoekhoe "Khoekhoe").[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Afonso_de_Albuquerque#cite_note-35) Upon his assuming office, Afonso intended to dominate the Muslim world and control the spice trade.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Afonso_de_Albuquerque#cite_note-Andaya-36)

Initially, King Manuel I and his council in Lisbon tried to distribute the power by outlining three areas of jurisdiction in the Indian Ocean.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Afonso_de_Albuquerque#cite_note-Foundations-6) In 1509, the nobleman [Diogo Lopes de Sequeira](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diogo_Lopes_de_Sequeira "Diogo Lopes de Sequeira") was sent with a fleet to Southeast Asia, to seek an agreement with [Sultan Mahmud Shah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sultan_Mahmud_Shah "Sultan Mahmud Shah") of [Malacca](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malacca "Malacca"), but failed and returned to Portugal. To Jorge de Aguiar was given the region between the [Cape of Good Hope](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cape_of_Good_Hope "Cape of Good Hope") and [Gujarat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gujarat "Gujarat"). He was succeeded by [Duarte de Lemos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Duarte_de_Lemos,_3rd_Lord_of_Trofa "Duarte de Lemos, 3rd Lord of Trofa"), but left for Cochin and then for Portugal, leaving his fleet to Afonso.

### Conquest of Goa, 1510

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Afonso_de_Albuquerque&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Conquest of Goa, 1510")]

Main article: [Portuguese Conquest of Goa (1510)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portuguese_Conquest_of_Goa_(1510) "Portuguese Conquest of Goa (1510)")

[![Image 12](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/4d/%22Plan_de_Goa%22%2C_in_Histoire_g%C3%A9n%C3%A9rale_des_voyages%2C1750.jpg/250px-%22Plan_de_Goa%22%2C_in_Histoire_g%C3%A9n%C3%A9rale_des_voyages%2C1750.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:%22Plan_de_Goa%22,_in_Histoire_g%C3%A9n%C3%A9rale_des_voyages,1750.jpg)

Illustration depicts the aftermath of the [Portuguese conquest of Goa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portuguese_conquest_of_Goa "Portuguese conquest of Goa"), from the forces of [Yusuf Adil Shah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yusuf_Adil_Shah "Yusuf Adil Shah").

In January 1510, obeying the orders from the king and aware of the absence of the [Zamorin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zamorin "Zamorin"), Afonso advanced on Calicut. The attack was initially successful, but unravelled when Marshal Coutinho, infuriated by Albuquerque's success against Calicut and desiring glory for himself, attacked the Zamorin's palace against Albuquerque's advice, and was ambushed. During the retreat, Afonso was badly wounded and was forced to flee to the ships, barely escaping with his life, while Coutinho was killed.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Afonso_de_Albuquerque#cite_note-Foundations-6)[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Afonso_de_Albuquerque#cite_note-37)

Soon after the failed attack, Afonso assembled a fleet of 23 ships and 1200 men. Contemporary reports state that he wanted to fight the [Egyptian Mamluk Sultanate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mamluk_Sultanate_(Cairo) "Mamluk Sultanate (Cairo)") fleet in the Red Sea or return to Hormuz. However, he had been informed by [Timoji](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timoji "Timoji") (a privateer in the service of the Hindu [Vijayanagara Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vijayanagara_Empire "Vijayanagara Empire")) that it would be easier to fight them in [Goa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Goa "Goa"), where they had sheltered after the Battle of Diu,[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Afonso_de_Albuquerque#cite_note-Shastry-38) and also of the illness of the Sultan [Yusuf Adil Shah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yusuf_Adil_Shah "Yusuf Adil Shah"), and war between the [Deccan sultanates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deccan_sultanates "Deccan sultanates").[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Afonso_de_Albuquerque#cite_note-Shastry-38) So he relied on surprise in the capture of Goa from the [Sultanate of Bijapur](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sultanate_of_Bijapur "Sultanate of Bijapur").

A first assault took place in Goa from 4 March to 20 May 1510. After the initial occupation, feeling unable to hold the city given the poor condition of its fortifications, the cooling of Hindu residents' support and insubordination among his ranks following an attack by [Ismail Adil Shah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ismail_Adil_Shah "Ismail Adil Shah"), Afonso refused a truce offered by the Sultan and abandoned the city in August. His fleet was scattered, and a palace revolt in Kochi hindered his recovery, so he headed to [Fort Anjediva](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fort_Anjediva "Fort Anjediva"). New ships arrived from Portugal, which were intended for the nobleman Diogo Mendes de Vasconcelos at Malacca, who had been given a rival command of the region.

Three months later, on 25 November Afonso reappeared at Goa with a renovated fleet. Diogo Mendes de Vasconcelos was compelled to accompany him with the reinforcements for Malacca[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Afonso_de_Albuquerque#cite_note-Foundations-6) and about 300 Malabari reinforcements from Cannanore. In less than a day, they took Goa from Ismail Adil Shah and his Ottoman allies, who surrendered on 10 December. It is estimated that 6000 of the 9000 Muslim defenders of the city died, either in the fierce battle in the streets or by drowning while trying to escape.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Afonso_de_Albuquerque#cite_note-39) Afonso regained the support of the Hindu population, although he frustrated the initial expectations of Timoji, who aspired to become governor. Afonso rewarded him by appointing him chief "[Aguazil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aguazil "Aguazil")" of the city, an administrator and representative of the Hindu and Muslim people, as a knowledgeable interpreter of the local customs.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Afonso_de_Albuquerque#cite_note-Shastry-38) He then made an agreement to lower the yearly tribute.

[![Image 13](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/thumb/5/52/Coining_of_money_for_D%27Albuquerque_at_Goa%2C_1510.jpg/250px-Coining_of_money_for_D%27Albuquerque_at_Goa%2C_1510.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Coining_of_money_for_D'Albuquerque_at_Goa,_1510.jpg)

Coining of money for d'Albuquerque at Goa (1510)

In Goa, Afonso established the first Portuguese mint in the East, after Timoja's merchants had complained of the scarcity of currency, taking it as an opportunity to solidify the territorial conquest.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Afonso_de_Albuquerque#cite_note-40) The new coin, based on the existing local coins, showed a cross on the obverse and an [armillary sphere](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Armillary_sphere "Armillary sphere") (or "esfera"), King Manuel's badge, on the reverse. Gold cruzados or _manueis_, silver _esferas_ and _alf-esferas_, and bronze "leais" were issued.[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Afonso_de_Albuquerque#cite_note-41)

Albuquerque founded at Goa the _Hospital Real de Goa_ or Royal Hospital of Goa, by the Church of Santa Catarina. Upon hearing that the doctors were extorting the sickly with excessive fees, Albuquerque summoned them, declaring that "You charge a physician's pay and don't know what disease the men who serve our lord the King suffer from. Thus, I want to teach you what is it that they die from"[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Afonso_de_Albuquerque#cite_note-42) and put them to work building the city walls all day till nightfall before releasing them.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Afonso_de_Albuquerque#cite_note-43)

Despite constant attacks, Goa became the center of Portuguese India, with the conquest triggering the compliance of neighbouring kingdoms: the [Sultan of Gujarat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sultan_of_Gujarat "Sultan of Gujarat") and the [Zamorin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zamorin "Zamorin") of Calicut sent embassies, offering alliances and local grants to fortify.

Afonso then used Goa to secure the spice trade in favor of Portugal and sell [Persian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Persia "Persia") horses to [Vijayanagara](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vijayanagara "Vijayanagara") and Hindu princes in return for their assistance.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Afonso_de_Albuquerque#cite_note-britannica.com-21)

### Conquest of Malacca, 1511

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Afonso_de_Albuquerque&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Conquest of Malacca, 1511")]

[![Image 14](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/e3/Iberian_mare_clausum_claims.svg/250px-Iberian_mare_clausum_claims.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Iberian_mare_clausum_claims.svg)

Map of the _[mare clausum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mare\_clausum "Mare clausum")_ claims made by [Spanish Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spanish_Empire "Spanish Empire") and [Portuguese Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portuguese_Empire "Portuguese Empire"), with Afonso's "Strait Controlling" strategy marked in blue circles.

Main article: [Portuguese Empire in the East](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portuguese_Empire_in_the_East "Portuguese Empire in the East")

Main article: [Capture of Malacca (1511)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capture_of_Malacca_(1511) "Capture of Malacca (1511)")

Afonso explained to his armies why the Portuguese wanted to capture Malacca:

"_The King of Portugal has often commanded me to go to the Straits, because...this was the best place to intercept the trade which the Moslems...carry on in these parts. So it was to do Our Lord's service that we were brought here; by taking Malacca, we would close the Straits so that never again would the Moslems be able to bring their spices by this route.... I am very sure that, if this Malacca trade is taken out of their hands, Cairo and Mecca will be completely lost._" (The Commentaries of the Great Afonso de Albuquerque)
In February 1511, through a friendly Hindu merchant, Nina Chatu, Afonso received a letter from Rui de Araújo, one of the nineteen Portuguese held at Malacca since 1509. It urged moving forward with the largest possible fleet to demand their release, and gave details of the fortifications. Afonso showed it to Diogo Mendes de Vasconcelos, as an argument to advance as a joint fleet. In April 1511, after fortifying Goa, he gathered a force of about 900 Portuguese, 200 Hindu mercenaries and about eighteen ships.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Afonso_de_Albuquerque#cite_note-RICKLEFSp23-44) He then sailed to [Malacca](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malacca_Sultanate "Malacca Sultanate") against orders and despite the protest of Diogo Mendes, who claimed command of the expedition. Afonso eventually centralized the Portuguese government in the Indian Ocean. After the Malaccan conquest, he wrote a letter to the king to explain his disagreement with Diogo Mendes, suggesting that further divisions could be harmful to the Portuguese in India.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Afonso_de_Albuquerque#cite_note-Foundations-6) Under his command was [Ferdinand Magellan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Magellan "Ferdinand Magellan"), who had participated in the failed embassy of Diogo Lopes de Sequeira in 1509.

[![Image 15](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/2e/Conquista_de_Malaca%2C_estudo_-_Ernesto_Condeixa.png/250px-Conquista_de_Malaca%2C_estudo_-_Ernesto_Condeixa.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Conquista_de_Malaca,_estudo_-_Ernesto_Condeixa.png)

"Conquest of Malacca", study painting by Ernesto Condeixa

After a false start towards the Red Sea, they sailed to the Strait of Malacca. It was the richest city that the Portuguese tried to take, and a focal point in the trade network where Malay traders met Gujarati, Chinese, Japanese, Javanese, Bengali, Persian and Arabic, among others, described by [Tomé Pires](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom%C3%A9_Pires "Tomé Pires") as of invaluable richness. Despite its wealth, it was mostly a wooden-built city, with few masonry buildings but was defended by a mercenary force estimated at 20,000 men and more than 2000 pieces of artillery. Its greatest weakness was the unpopularity of the government of [Sultan Mahmud Shah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sultan_Mahmud_Shah "Sultan Mahmud Shah"), who favoured Muslims, arousing dissatisfaction amongst other merchants.

Afonso made a bold approach to the city, his ships decorated with banners, firing cannon volleys. He declared himself lord of all the navigation, demanded the Sultan release the prisoners and pay for damages, and demanded consent to build a fortified trading post. The Sultan eventually freed the prisoners, but was unimpressed by the small Portuguese contingent. Afonso then burned some ships at the port and four coastal buildings as a demonstration. The city being divided by the Malacca River, the connecting bridge was a strategic point, so at dawn on 25 July, the Portuguese landed and fought a tough battle, facing poisoned arrows, taking the bridge in the evening. After fruitlessly waiting for the Sultan's reaction, they returned to the ships and prepared a [junk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Junk_(ship) "Junk (ship)") (offered by Chinese merchants), filling it with men, artillery and sandbags. Commanded by [António de Abreu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ant%C3%B3nio_de_Abreu "António de Abreu"), it sailed upriver at high tide to the bridge. The day after, all had landed. After a fierce fight during which the Sultan appeared with an army of war elephants, the defenders were dispersed and the Sultan fled.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Afonso_de_Albuquerque#cite_note-Foundations-6) Afonso waited for the reaction of the Sultan. Merchants approached, asking for Portuguese protection. They were given banners to mark their premises, a sign that they would not be looted. On 15 August, the Portuguese attacked again, but the Sultan had fled the city. Under strict orders, they looted the city, but respected the banners.[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Afonso_de_Albuquerque#cite_note-Bosworth2007-45)

[![Image 16](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/84/Manuel_Godinho_de_Er%C3%A9dia_-_Description_of_Malacca%2C_Meridional_India_and_Cathay_-_A_Famosa.png/250px-Manuel_Godinho_de_Er%C3%A9dia_-_Description_of_Malacca%2C_Meridional_India_and_Cathay_-_A_Famosa.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Manuel_Godinho_de_Er%C3%A9dia_-_Description_of_Malacca,_Meridional_India_and_Cathay_-_A_Famosa.png)

An illustration of the keep of the fortress of Malacca, which included a stone relief of Afonso de Albuquerque, by [Manuel Godinho de Erédia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manuel_Godinho_de_Er%C3%A9dia "Manuel Godinho de Erédia") (1613)

[![Image 17](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/69/Malacca_in_1550-1563.png/250px-Malacca_in_1550-1563.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Malacca_in_1550-1563.png)

Malacca, with [A Famosa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_Famosa "A Famosa"), depicted by Albuquerque's scrivener, [Gaspar Correia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gaspar_Correia "Gaspar Correia"). 

Afonso prepared Malacca's defenses against a Malay counterattack,[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Afonso_de_Albuquerque#cite_note-RICKLEFSp23-44) building a fortress, assigning his men to shifts and using stones from the mosque and the cemetery. Despite the delays caused by heat and malaria, it was completed in November 1511, its surviving door now known as "[A Famosa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_Famosa "A Famosa")" ('the famous'). It was possibly then that Afonso had a large stone engraved with the names of the participants in the conquest. To quell disagreements over the order of the names, he had it set facing the wall, with the single inscription _Lapidem quem reprobaverunt aedificantes_ (Latin for "The stone the builders rejected", from [David](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David "David")'s prophecy, Psalm 118:22–23) on the front.[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Afonso_de_Albuquerque#cite_note-46)

He settled the Portuguese administration, reappointing Rui de Araújo as [factor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Factor_(agent) "Factor (agent)"), a post assigned before his 1509 arrest, and appointing rich merchant Nina Chatu to replace the previous [Bendahara](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bendahara "Bendahara"). Besides assisting in the governance of the city and the first Portuguese coinage, he provided the junks for several diplomatic missions.[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Afonso_de_Albuquerque#cite_note-47) Meanwhile, Afonso arrested and had executed the powerful Javanese merchant Utimuti Raja who, after being appointed to a position in the Portuguese administration as representative of the Javanese population, had maintained contacts with the exiled royal family.

#### Shipwreck on the _Flor de la mar_, 1511

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Afonso_de_Albuquerque&action=edit&section=11 "Edit section: Shipwreck on the Flor de la mar, 1511")]

[![Image 18](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/fc/Portuguese_ship_museum_Melaka.jpg/250px-Portuguese_ship_museum_Melaka.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Portuguese_ship_museum_Melaka.jpg)

Replica of a Portuguese carrack at the Maritime Museum of Malacca, made in reference to the Flor do Mar

On 20 November 1511 Afonso sailed from Malacca to the coast of Malabar on the old _[Flor de la Mar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flor\_de\_la\_Mar "Flor de la Mar")_[carrack](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carrack "Carrack") that had served to support the conquest of Malacca. Despite its unsound condition, he used it to transport the treasure amassed in the conquest, given its large capacity.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Afonso_de_Albuquerque#cite_note-Foundations-6) He wanted to give the court of King Manuel a show of Malaccan treasures. There were also offerings from the [Ayutthaya Kingdom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ayutthaya_Kingdom "Ayutthaya Kingdom") (Thailand) to the king of Portugal, and all his own fortune. On the voyage, the _[Flor de la Mar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flor\_de\_la\_Mar "Flor de la Mar")_ was wrecked in a storm, and Afonso barely escaped drowning.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Afonso_de_Albuquerque#cite_note-RICKLEFSp23-44)

### Missions from Malacca

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Afonso_de_Albuquerque&action=edit&section=12 "Edit section: Missions from Malacca")]

#### Embassies to Pegu, Sumatra and Siam, 1511

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Afonso_de_Albuquerque&action=edit&section=13 "Edit section: Embassies to Pegu, Sumatra and Siam, 1511")]

Most Muslim and Gujarati merchants having fled the city, Afonso invested in diplomatic efforts demonstrating generosity to Southeast Asian merchants, like the Chinese, to encourage good relations with the Portuguese. Trade and diplomatic missions were sent to continental kingdoms: Rui Nunes da Cunha was sent to [Pegu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pegu "Pegu") (Burma), from where King Binyaram sent back a friendly emissary to Kochi in 1514[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Afonso_de_Albuquerque#cite_note-48)[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Afonso_de_Albuquerque#cite_note-49) and [Sumatra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sumatra "Sumatra"), Sumatran kings of Kampar and Indragiri sending emissaries to Afonso accepting the new power, as vassal states of Malacca.[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Afonso_de_Albuquerque#cite_note-Lach-50) Knowing of Siamese ambitions over Malacca, Afonso sent [Duarte Fernandes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Duarte_Fernandes "Duarte Fernandes") in a diplomatic mission to the [Ayutthaya Kingdom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ayutthaya_Kingdom "Ayutthaya Kingdom") (Thailand), returning in a Chinese junk. He was one of the Portuguese who had been arrested in Malacca, having gathered knowledge about the culture of the region. There he was the first European to arrive, establishing amicable relations between the kingdom of Portugal and the court of the king of Siam [Ramathibodi II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ramathibodi_II "Ramathibodi II"), returning with a Siamese envoy bearing gifts and letters to Afonso and the king of Portugal.[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Afonso_de_Albuquerque#cite_note-Lach-50)

#### Expedition to the "spice islands" (Maluku islands), 1512

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Afonso_de_Albuquerque&action=edit&section=14 "Edit section: Expedition to the \"spice islands\" (Maluku islands), 1512")]

[![Image 19](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/3f/Ternate.JPG/250px-Ternate.JPG?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Ternate.JPG)

Depiction of [Ternate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ternate "Ternate") with São João Baptista Fort, built in 1522

In November, after having secured Malacca and learning the location of the then secret "[spice islands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maluku_Islands "Maluku Islands")", Afonso sent three ships to find them, led by trusted [António de Abreu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ant%C3%B3nio_de_Abreu "António de Abreu") with deputy commander [Francisco Serrão](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Francisco_Serr%C3%A3o "Francisco Serrão").[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Afonso_de_Albuquerque#cite_note-51)[Malay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malay_(ethnic_group) "Malay (ethnic group)") sailors were recruited to guide them through [Java](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Java "Java"), the [Lesser Sunda Islands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lesser_Sunda_Islands "Lesser Sunda Islands") and the [Ambon Island](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ambon_Island "Ambon Island") to [Banda Islands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Banda_Islands "Banda Islands"), where they arrived in early 1512.[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Afonso_de_Albuquerque#cite_note-Milton_1999_5_and_7-52) There they remained for a month, buying and filling their ships with nutmeg and cloves. António de Abreu then sailed to Amboina whilst Serrão sailed towards the Moluccas, but he was shipwrecked near Seram. [Sultan Abu Lais of Ternate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sultanate_of_Ternate "Sultanate of Ternate") heard of their stranding, and, seeing a chance to ally himself with a powerful foreign nation, brought them to Ternate in 1512 where they were permitted to build a fort on the island, the _[Forte de São João Baptista de Ternate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Forte\_de\_S%C3%A3o\_Jo%C3%A3o\_Baptista\_de\_Ternate "Forte de São João Baptista de Ternate")_, built in 1522.

### Return to Cochin and Goa

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Afonso_de_Albuquerque&action=edit&section=15 "Edit section: Return to Cochin and Goa")]

Afonso returned from Malacca to Cochin, but could not sail to Goa as it faced a serious revolt headed by the forces of [Ismael Adil Shah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ismael_Adil_Shah "Ismael Adil Shah"), the Sultan of [Bijapur](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adil_Shahi_dynasty "Adil Shahi dynasty"), commanded by [Rasul Khan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rasul_Khan "Rasul Khan") and his countrymen. During Afonso's absence from Malacca, the Portuguese who opposed the taking of Goa had waived its possession, even writing to the king that it would be best to let it go. Held up by the monsoon and with few forces available, Afonso had to wait for the arrival of reinforcement fleets headed by his nephew D. Garcia de Noronha, and Jorge de Mello Pereira.

While at Cochin, Albuquerque started a school. In a private letter to King Manuel I, he stated that he had found a chest full of books with which to teach the children of married Portuguese settlers (_casados_) and Christian converts, of which there were about a hundred, to read and write.[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Afonso_de_Albuquerque#cite_note-53)

On 10 September 1512, Afonso sailed from Cochin to Goa with fourteen ships carrying 1,700 soldiers. Determined to recapture the fortress, he ordered trenches dug and a wall breached. But on the day of the planned final assault, Rasul Khan surrendered. Afonso demanded the fort be handed over with its artillery, ammunition and horses, and the deserters to be given up. Some had joined Rasul Khan when the Portuguese were forced to flee Goa in May 1510, others during the recent siege. Rasul Khan consented, on condition that their lives be spared. Afonso agreed and he left Goa. He did spare the lives of the deserters, but had them horribly mutilated. One such renegade was [Fernão Lopes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fern%C3%A3o_Lopes_(soldier) "Fernão Lopes (soldier)"), bound for Portugal in custody, who escaped at the island of Saint Helena and led a 'Robinson Crusoe' life for many years. After such measures the town became the most prosperous Portuguese settlement in India.

## Administration and diplomacy, 1512–1515

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Afonso_de_Albuquerque&action=edit&section=16 "Edit section: Administration and diplomacy, 1512–1515")]

### Ethiopian embassy, 1512

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Afonso_de_Albuquerque&action=edit&section=17 "Edit section: Ethiopian embassy, 1512")]

[![Image 20](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/56/Attempted_Escalade_of_Aden.jpg/250px-Attempted_Escalade_of_Aden.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Attempted_Escalade_of_Aden.jpg)

Attempted Portuguese scaling of the walls of Aden

In December 1512 an envoy from Ethiopia arrived at Goa. [Mateus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mateus_(Ethiopia) "Mateus (Ethiopia)") was sent by the regent queen [Eleni](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eleni_of_Ethiopia "Eleni of Ethiopia"), following the arrival of the Portuguese from Socotra in 1507, as an ambassador for the king of Portugal in search of a coalition to help face growing Muslim influence. He was received in Goa with great honour by Afonso, as a long-sought "[Prester John](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prester_John "Prester John")" envoy. His arrival was announced by King Manuel to [Pope Leo X](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pope_Leo_X "Pope Leo X") in 1513. Although Mateus faced the distrust of Afonso's rivals, who tried to prove he was some impostor or Muslim spy, Afonso sent him to Portugal.[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Afonso_de_Albuquerque#cite_note-54) The king is described as having wept with joy at their report.

In February 1513, while Mateus was in Portugal, Afonso sailed to the Red Sea with a force of about 1000 Portuguese and 400 Malabaris. He was under orders to secure that channel for Portugal. Socotra had proved ineffective to control the Red Sea entrance and was abandoned, and Afonso's hint that [Massawa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Massawa "Massawa") could be a good Portuguese base might have been influenced by Mateus' reports.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Afonso_de_Albuquerque#cite_note-Foundations-6)

### Campaign in the Red Sea, 1513

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Afonso_de_Albuquerque&action=edit&section=18 "Edit section: Campaign in the Red Sea, 1513")]

Knowing that the Mamluks were preparing a second fleet at [Suez](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Suez "Suez"), he wanted to advance before reinforcements arrived in [Aden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aden "Aden"), and accordingly [laid siege to the city](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Aden_(1513) "Siege of Aden (1513)").[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Afonso_de_Albuquerque#cite_note-55) Aden was a fortified city, but although he had scaling ladders they broke during the chaotic attack. After half a day of fierce battle, Afonso was forced to retreat. He cruised the Red Sea inside the [Bab al-Mandab](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bab_al-Mandab "Bab al-Mandab"), with the first European fleet to have sailed this route. He attempted to reach [Jeddah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeddah "Jeddah"), but the winds were unfavourable and so he sheltered at [Kamaran](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kamaran "Kamaran") island in May, until sickness among the men and lack of fresh water forced him to retreat. In August 1513, after a second attempt to reach Aden, he returned to India with no substantial results. In order to destroy the power of Egypt, he wrote to King Manuel of the idea of diverting the course of the [Nile](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nile "Nile") river to render the whole country barren.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Afonso_de_Albuquerque#cite_note-Chisholm-8) He also intended to steal the body of the Islamic prophet, [Muhammad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muhammad "Muhammad"), and hold it for ransom until all Muslims had left the [Holy Land](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Holy_Land "Holy Land").[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Afonso_de_Albuquerque#cite_note-56)

[![Image 21](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/3d/Afonso_de_Albuquerque_%28Sloane%29.jpg/250px-Afonso_de_Albuquerque_%28Sloane%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Afonso_de_Albuquerque_(Sloane).jpg)

Portrait of Afonso de Albuquerque, governor of Portuguese Indies (1509–1515), from Pedro Barretto de Resende's Livro de Estado da India Oriental

Although Albuquerque's expedition failed to reach Suez, such an incursion into the Red Sea by a Christian fleet for the first time in history stunned the Muslim world, and panic spread in Cairo.[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Afonso_de_Albuquerque#cite_note-57)

### Submission of Calicut

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Afonso_de_Albuquerque&action=edit&section=19 "Edit section: Submission of Calicut")]

See also: [First Luso-Malabarese War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_Luso-Malabarese_War "First Luso-Malabarese War")

[![Image 22](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/cd/Portuguese_fort_at_Calicut_%28cropped%29.jpg/250px-Portuguese_fort_at_Calicut_%28cropped%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Portuguese_fort_at_Calicut_(cropped).jpg)

The Portuguese fort at Calicut

Albuquerque achieved during his term a favourable end to hostilities between the Portuguese and the Zamorin of Calicut, which had lasted since the massacre of the Portuguese in Calicut in 1502. As naval trade faltered and vassals defected, with no foreseeable solutions to the conflict with the Portuguese, the court of the Zamorin fell to in-fighting. The ruling Zamorin was assassinated and replaced by a rival, under the instigation of Albuquerque, permitting peace talks to commence. The Portuguese were allowed to build a fortress in Calicut itself, and acquired rights to obtain as much pepper and ginger as they wished, at stipulated prices, and half the [customs duties](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Customs_duties "Customs duties") of Calicut as yearly tribute.[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Afonso_de_Albuquerque#cite_note-58) Construction of the fortress began immediately, under the supervision of chief architect Tomás Fernandes.

### Goa, 1514

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Afonso_de_Albuquerque&action=edit&section=20 "Edit section: Goa, 1514")]

[![Image 23](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c1/Codice_Casanatense_Portuguese_Nobleman_and_Christian_Indian.jpg/250px-Codice_Casanatense_Portuguese_Nobleman_and_Christian_Indian.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Codice_Casanatense_Portuguese_Nobleman_and_Christian_Indian.jpg)

Christian maidens of Goa, meeting with a Portuguese nobleman seeking a wife (depicted in the [Códice Casanatense](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/C%C3%B3dice_Casanatense "Códice Casanatense"), c.1540)

With peace concluded, in 1514 Afonso devoted himself to governing Goa and receiving embassies from Indian governors, strengthening the city and encouraging marriages of Portuguese men and local women. At that time, Portuguese women were barred from traveling overseas in order to maintain discipline among the men on board the ships. In 1511 under a policy which Afonso promulgated, the Portuguese government encouraged their explorers to marry local women. To promote settlement, the King of Portugal granted freeman status and exemption from Crown taxes to Portuguese men (known as _casados_, or "married men") who ventured overseas and married local women. With Afonso's encouragement, mixed marriages flourished, giving birth to Portuguese-Indians or _[mestiços](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mesti%C3%A7o#Mesti%C3%A7o\_communities\_in\_Portuguese\_India\_and\_Portuguese\_Ceylon "Mestiço")_. He appointed local people for positions in the Portuguese administration and did not interfere with local traditions (except "[sati](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sati_(practice) "Sati (practice)")", the practice of immolating widows, which he banned).

In March 1514 King Manuel sent to [Pope Leo X](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pope_Leo_X "Pope Leo X") an embassy led by [Tristão da Cunha](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trist%C3%A3o_da_Cunha "Tristão da Cunha"), who toured the streets of Rome in an extravagant procession of animals from the colonies and wealth from the Indies. His reputation reached its peak, laying foundations of the Portuguese Empire in the East.

[![Image 24](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/3f/D%C3%BCrer%27s_Rhinoceros%2C_1515.jpg/250px-D%C3%BCrer%27s_Rhinoceros%2C_1515.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:D%C3%BCrer's_Rhinoceros,_1515.jpg)

[Dürer's Rhinoceros](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/D%C3%BCrer's_Rhinoceros "Dürer's Rhinoceros"), [woodcut](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Woodcut "Woodcut") (1515)

In early 1514, Afonso sent ambassadors to [Gujarat's Sultan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sultan_of_Gujarat "Sultan of Gujarat")[Muzaffar Shah II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muzaffar_Shah_II "Muzaffar Shah II"), ruler of [Cambay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cambay "Cambay"), to seek permission to build a fort on [Diu, India](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diu,_India "Diu, India"). The mission returned without an agreement, but diplomatic gifts were exchanged, including an Indian rhinoceros.[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Afonso_de_Albuquerque#cite_note-59) Afonso sent the rhino to King Manuel, making it the first living example of a rhinoceros seen in Europe since the Roman Empire.[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Afonso_de_Albuquerque#cite_note-60) King Manuel named the rhino Genda after the Gujarat word for ball, and later gifted it to Pope Leo X, but before completing its journey to Italy the boat carrying the rhino sank and the animal drowned. In 1515, German artist [Albrecht Dürer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Albrecht_D%C3%BCrer "Albrecht Dürer") created his famous woodcut known as [Dürer's Rhinoceros](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/D%C3%BCrer's_Rhinoceros "Dürer's Rhinoceros"), based on a description from a letter and a brief sketch made by an unknown artist who had seen the actual animal. Dürer's interpretation of the rhino cemented the idea of how a rhino should look like in people's mindsets up until the late-eighteenth century.[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Afonso_de_Albuquerque#cite_note-61)

### Conquest of Ormuz and Illness

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Afonso_de_Albuquerque&action=edit&section=21 "Edit section: Conquest of Ormuz and Illness")]

[![Image 25](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/c/c4/Afonso_de_Albuquerque_%28Livro_de_Lisuarte_de_Abreu%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail_unscaled)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Afonso_de_Albuquerque_(Livro_de_Lisuarte_de_Abreu).jpg)

Portrait of Afonso de Albuquerque, from the _Livro de Lisuarte de Abreu_ (c.1565)

In 1513, at Cannanore, Afonso was visited by a Persian ambassador from Shah [Ismail I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ismail_I "Ismail I"), who had sent ambassadors to Gujarat, [Ormuz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ormuz "Ormuz") and Bijapur. The shah's ambassador to Bijapur invited Afonso to send back an envoy to Persia. Miguel Ferreira was sent via Ormuz to [Tabriz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tabriz "Tabriz"), where he had several interviews with the shah about common goals of defeating the Mamluk sultan.

At the same time, Albuquerque decided to conclude the effective conquest of Hormuz. He had learned that after the Portuguese retreat in 1507, a young king was reigning under the influence of a powerful Persian [vizier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vizier "Vizier"), Reis Hamed, whom the king greatly feared. At Ormuz in March 1515, Afonso met the king and asked the vizier to be present. He then had him immediately stabbed and killed by his entourage, thus "freeing" the terrified king, so the island in the Persian Gulf yielded to him without resistance and remained a vassal state of the Portuguese Empire. Ormuz itself would not be Persian territory for another century, until an English-Persian alliance finally expelled the Portuguese in 1622.[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Afonso_de_Albuquerque#cite_note-intlhistory.blogspot.com.au-62) At Ormuz, Afonso met with Miguel Ferreira, returning with rich presents and an ambassador, carrying a letter from the Persian potentate Shah Ismael, inviting Afonso to become a leading lord in Persia.[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Afonso_de_Albuquerque#cite_note-63) There he remained, engaging in diplomatic efforts, receiving envoys and overseeing the construction of the new fortress, while becoming increasingly ill. His illness was reported as early as September 1515.[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Afonso_de_Albuquerque#cite_note-Early-64) In November 1515, he embarked on a journey back to Goa.

#### Death

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Afonso_de_Albuquerque&action=edit&section=22 "Edit section: Death")]

At this time, his political enemies at the Portuguese court were planning his downfall. They had lost no opportunity in stirring up the jealousy of King Manuel against him, insinuating that Afonso intended to usurp power in Portuguese India.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Afonso_de_Albuquerque#cite_note-Albuquerque-17) While on his return voyage from Ormuz in the Persian Gulf, near the harbor of [Chaul](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chaul "Chaul"), he received news of a Portuguese fleet arriving from Europe, bearing dispatches announcing that he was to be replaced by his personal foe, [Lopo Soares de Albergaria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lopo_Soares_de_Albergaria "Lopo Soares de Albergaria"). Realizing the plot that his enemies had moved against him, profoundly disillusioned, he voiced his bitterness: "Grave must be my sins before the King, for I am in ill favor with the King for love of the men, and with the men for love of the King."[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Afonso_de_Albuquerque#cite_note-65)

Feeling himself near death, he donned the surcoat of the [Order of Santiago](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Military_Order_of_Saint_James_of_the_Sword "Military Order of Saint James of the Sword"), of which he was a knight, and drew up his will, appointed the captain and senior officials of Ormuz, and organized a final council with his captains to decide the main matters affecting the Portuguese State of India.[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Afonso_de_Albuquerque#cite_note-Early-64) He wrote a brief letter to King Manuel, asking him to confer onto his natural son "all of the high honors and rewards" that Afonso had received, and assuring Manuel of his loyalty.[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Afonso_de_Albuquerque#cite_note-intlhistory.blogspot.com.au-62)[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Afonso_de_Albuquerque#cite_note-66)

On 16 December 1515, Afonso de Albuquerque died within sight of Goa. As his death was known, in the city "great wailing arose",[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Afonso_de_Albuquerque#cite_note-Corr459-67) and many took to the streets to witness his body carried on a chair by his main captains, in a procession lit by torches amidst the crowd.[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Afonso_de_Albuquerque#cite_note-68) Afonso's body was buried in Goa, according to his will, in the Church of Nossa Senhora da Serra (Our Lady of the Hill), which he had been built in 1513 to thank the Madonna for his escape from [Kamaran](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kamaran "Kamaran") island.[[a]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Afonso_de_Albuquerque#cite_note-70) That night, the population of Goa, both Hindu and Portuguese, gathered to mourn his death.[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Afonso_de_Albuquerque#cite_note-Corr459-67)

In Portugal, King Manuel's zigzagging policies continued, still trapped by the constraints of real-time medieval communication between Lisbon and India and unaware that Afonso was dead. Hearing rumours that the [Mamluk Sultan of Egypt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mamluk_Sultanate_(Cairo) "Mamluk Sultanate (Cairo)") was preparing a magnificent army at Suez to prevent the conquest of Ormuz, he repented of having replaced Afonso, and in March 1516 urgently wrote to Albergaria to return the command of all operations to Afonso and provide him with resources to face the Egyptian threat. He organized a new Portuguese navy in Asia, with orders that Afonso (if he was still in India), be made commander-in-chief against the Sultan of Cairo's armies. Manuel would afterwards learn that Afonso had died many months earlier, and that his reversed decision had been delivered many months too late.[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Afonso_de_Albuquerque#cite_note-Early-64)[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Afonso_de_Albuquerque#cite_note-Albuquerque-17)

After 51 years, in 1566, his body was moved to Nossa Senhora da Graça church in Lisbon,[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Afonso_de_Albuquerque#cite_note-71) which was ruined and rebuilt after the [1755 Great Lisbon earthquake](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1755_Lisbon_earthquake "1755 Lisbon earthquake").

Afonso de Albuquerque as governor of India

King Manuel I of Portugal was belatedly convinced of Afonso's loyalty, and endeavoured to atone for his lack of confidence in Afonso by heaping honours upon his son, [Brás de Albuquerque](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Br%C3%A1s_de_Albuquerque?action=edit&redlink=1 "Brás de Albuquerque (page does not exist)") (1500–1580),[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Afonso_de_Albuquerque#cite_note-72) whom he renamed "Afonso" in memory of the father. Afonso de Albuquerque was a prolific writer, having sent numerous letters during his governorship, covering topics from minor issues to major strategies. In 1557 his son published his biography under the title _Commentarios do Grande Affonso d'Alboquerque_.[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Afonso_de_Albuquerque#cite_note-73)

In 1572, Afonso's actions were described in _[The Lusiads](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Lusiads "The Lusiads")_, the Portuguese main epic poem by [Luís Vaz de Camões](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lu%C3%ADs_de_Cam%C3%B5es "Luís de Camões") (Canto X, strophes 40–49). The poet praises his achievements, but has the [muses](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muses "Muses") frown upon the harsh rule of his men, of whom Camões was almost a contemporary fellow. In 1934, Afonso was celebrated by [Fernando Pessoa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fernando_Pessoa "Fernando Pessoa") in _Mensagem_, a [symbolist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Symbolism_(arts) "Symbolism (arts)") epic. In the first part of this work, called "Brasão" (Coat-of-Arms), he relates Portuguese historical protagonists to each of the fields in the Portuguese coat-of-arms, Afonso being one of the wings of the [griffin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Griffin "Griffin") headed by Henry the Navigator, the other wing being King John II.

A [variety of mango](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alphonso_(mango) "Alphonso (mango)"), which was created by Portuguese [Jesuits](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jesuits "Jesuits") in Goa via [grafting](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grafting "Grafting") techniques, was named in his honour.[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Afonso_de_Albuquerque#cite_note-guard-74)[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Afonso_de_Albuquerque#cite_note-Alvares-75)

Numerous homages have been paid to Afonso. He is featured in the [Padrão dos Descobrimentos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Padr%C3%A3o_dos_Descobrimentos "Padrão dos Descobrimentos") monument. There is a [square named after him](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Afonso_de_Albuquerque_Square "Afonso de Albuquerque Square") in [Lisbon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lisbon "Lisbon"), which also features a bronze statue, as well as a prominent statue of his enrobed figure in a garden square in Bairro Gomes da Costa in Porto.

Two Portuguese Navy ships have been named in his honour: the sloop [NRP _Afonso de Albuquerque_ (1884)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Afonso_de_Albuquerque_(1884) "Afonso de Albuquerque (1884)") and the warship [NRP _Afonso de Albuquerque_ (1934)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NRP_Afonso_de_Albuquerque_(1934) "NRP Afonso de Albuquerque (1934)").

The Albuquerque monument in front of the Belém Palace

**Afonso de Albuquerque Square** ([Portuguese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portuguese_language "Portuguese language"): _Praça Afonso de Albuquerque_) is a public square in the [Belém district](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bel%C3%A9m_(Lisbon) "Belém (Lisbon)") of the city of [Lisbon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lisbon "Lisbon"), [Portugal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portugal "Portugal").

## History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Afonso_de_Albuquerque_Square&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History")]

The square is located in front of [Belém Palace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bel%C3%A9m_Palace "Belém Palace"), an early 18th-century palace that nowadays serves as residence for the [President of Portugal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/President_of_Portugal "President of Portugal"). The square is named after the Second Governor of [Portuguese India](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portuguese_India "Portuguese India")Afonso de Albuquerque, and offers views of Belém Palace. It has a monument, in neo-[Manueline](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manueline "Manueline") style, by artists _Silva Pinto_ and _Costa Mota tio_, inaugurated in 1902. The monument carries a bronze statue of Afonso de Albuquerque and has reliefs about his life.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Afonso_de_Albuquerque_Square#cite_note-1)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Afonso_de_Albuquerque_Square#cite_note-2)

The site of the square used to be a harbour, built in 1753. In 1807, [Queen Mary I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maria_I_of_Portugal "Maria I of Portugal"), [Prince John VI](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_VI_of_Portugal "John VI of Portugal") and the [royal family fled Lisbon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transfer_of_the_Portuguese_Court_to_Brazil "Transfer of the Portuguese Court to Brazil") from this harbour to [Rio de Janeiro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rio_de_Janeiro "Rio de Janeiro"), in [Brazil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brazil "Brazil"), to escape the [Napoleonic troops](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Napoleon "Napoleon") which had [invaded Portugal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peninsular_War "Peninsular War").

Notable buildings include [Belém Palace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bel%C3%A9m_Palace "Belém Palace") and the [Nacional Coach Museum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Coach_Museum_(Lisbon) "National Coach Museum (Lisbon)").

**Afonso de Albuquerque Square** ([Portuguese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portuguese_language "Portuguese language"): _Praça Afonso de Albuquerque_) is a public square in the [Belém district](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bel%C3%A9m_(Lisbon) "Belém (Lisbon)") of the city of [Lisbon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lisbon "Lisbon"), [Portugal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portugal "Portugal").

## History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Afonso_de_Albuquerque_Square&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History")]

The square is located in front of [Belém Palace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bel%C3%A9m_Palace "Belém Palace"), an early 18th-century palace that nowadays serves as residence for the [President of Portugal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/President_of_Portugal "President of Portugal"). The square is named after the Second Governor of [Portuguese India](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portuguese_India "Portuguese India")Afonso de Albuquerque, and offers views of Belém Palace. It has a monument, in neo-[Manueline](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manueline "Manueline") style, by artists _Silva Pinto_ and _Costa Mota tio_, inaugurated in 1902. The monument carries a bronze statue of Afonso de Albuquerque and has reliefs about his life.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Afonso_de_Albuquerque_Square#cite_note-1)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Afonso_de_Albuquerque_Square#cite_note-2)

The site of the square used to be a harbour, built in 1753. In 1807, [Queen Mary I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maria_I_of_Portugal "Maria I of Portugal"), [Prince John VI](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_VI_of_Portugal "John VI of Portugal") and the [royal family fled Lisbon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transfer_of_the_Portuguese_Court_to_Brazil "Transfer of the Portuguese Court to Brazil") from this harbour to [Rio de Janeiro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rio_de_Janeiro "Rio de Janeiro"), in [Brazil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brazil "Brazil"), to escape the [Napoleonic troops](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Napoleon "Napoleon") which had [invaded Portugal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peninsular_War "Peninsular War").

Notable buildings include [Belém Palace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bel%C3%A9m_Palace "Belém Palace") and the [Nacional Coach Museum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Coach_Museum_(Lisbon) "National Coach Museum (Lisbon)").

**Diogo Cão** (European Portuguese pronunciation:[[diˈoɣu ˈkɐ̃w]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/Portuguese "Help:IPA/Portuguese"); c.1452 – 1486), also known as **Diogo Cam**, was a Portuguese mariner and one of the most notable explorers of the fifteenth century. He made two voyages along the west coast of Africa in the 1480s, exploring the [Congo River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Congo_River "Congo River") and the coasts of present-day Angola and Namibia.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diogo_C%C3%A3o#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDutra2007-1)

## Early life and family

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Diogo_C%C3%A3o&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Early life and family")]

Little is known about the early life of Diogo Cão. According to tradition, he was born in [Vila Real, Portugal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vila_Real,_Portugal "Vila Real, Portugal"), around 1452. His grandfather, Gonçalo Cão, had fought for Portuguese independence at the [Battle of Aljubarrota](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Aljubarrota "Battle of Aljubarrota").

By 1480, Cão was sailing off the coast of Africa in the service of [João II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jo%C3%A3o_II "João II"). There is a record that he returned to Portugal with captured Spanish ships.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diogo_C%C3%A3o#cite_note-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diogo_C%C3%A3o#cite_note-3)

## Exploration

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Diogo_C%C3%A3o&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Exploration")]

[![Image 5](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/4/48/Portuguese_discoveries_diogo_cao_cropped.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail_unscaled)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Portuguese_discoveries_diogo_cao_cropped.jpg)

Diogo Cão, at the mouth of Zaire, after having put the _padrão_

When the [Treaty of Alcáçovas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treaty_of_Alc%C3%A1%C3%A7ovas "Treaty of Alcáçovas") (1480) confirmed Portugal's monopoly on trade and exploration along Africa's west coast, João II moved quickly to secure and expand his hold on the region. In 1481, a fleet of ten ships was dispatched to the Gold Coast to construct a fortress known as [São Jorge da Mina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/S%C3%A3o_Jorge_da_Mina "São Jorge da Mina"). The fort would serve as a commercial center for trade (including in slaves) and an important point of resupply for Portuguese voyages. João II also re-instituted a program of exploration southward along the African coast, an initiative that had been held in abeyance during the war with Spain. Diogo Cão was selected to lead João's first voyage of exploration in 1482.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diogo_C%C3%A3o#cite_note-4)

### First voyage

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Diogo_C%C3%A3o&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: First voyage")]

[![Image 6](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/66/Caopillar.JPG/250px-Caopillar.JPG?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Caopillar.JPG)

The _padrão_ bearing the arms of Portugal erected by Cão at Cape St. Mary

When [João II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jo%C3%A3o_II "João II") restarted the work of [Henry the Navigator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_the_Navigator "Henry the Navigator"), he sent out Cão, probably around midsummer 1482, to explore the African coast south of the equator. Diogo Cão filled his ship with stone pillars (_[padrões](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Padr%C3%A3o "Padrão")_) surmounted by the cross of the Order of Christ and engraved with the Portuguese royal arms, planning to erect them at significant landmarks along his voyage of discovery.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diogo_C%C3%A3o#cite_note-FOOTNOTERavenstein1900627%E2%80%93628-5) On the way, the expedition stopped at Sao Jorge da Mina to resupply.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diogo_C%C3%A3o#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHowgego2003185-6)

In August 1482, Cão arrived at the Congo River mouth and marked it with a padrão erected on Shark Point, commemorating the Portuguese occupation. This padrão stood until 1642 when it was destroyed by the Dutch during their occupation of the Congo.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diogo_C%C3%A3o#cite_note-FOOTNOTERavenstein1900630-7)

Cão sailed up the great river for a short distance and commenced modest commerce with the natives of the [Bakongo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingdom_of_Kongo "Kingdom of Kongo") kingdom. He was told that their king lived farther upriver, so he sent four Christian native messengers to search for the ruler and then proceeded south along the coast of present-day Angola where he erected a second _padrão_, probably marking the termination of this voyage, at [Cabo de Santa Maria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cabo_de_Santa_Maria_(Angola) "Cabo de Santa Maria (Angola)"). When he returned to the Congo, Cão was annoyed to find that his messengers had not returned, so he abducted four local natives who were visiting his ship and returned with them to Portugal.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diogo_C%C3%A3o#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHowgego2003185-6)

[![Image 7](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/47/Armas_Diogo_C%C3%A3o.jpg/250px-Armas_Diogo_C%C3%A3o.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Armas_Diogo_C%C3%A3o.jpg)

Diogo Cão's coat of arms

He reached Lisbon by 8 April 1484, where John II ennobled him, promoting him from esquire to a cavalier of his household,[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diogo_C%C3%A3o#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHowgego2003185-6) and granted him an annuity of eighteen thousand _reals_ and a coat of arms on which two _padrões_ are depicted.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diogo_C%C3%A3o#cite_note-FOOTNOTERavenstein1900107-8)

The King also asked him to sail back to Kongo to repatriate the 4 men he left behind.

### Second voyage

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Diogo_C%C3%A3o&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Second voyage")]

[![Image 8](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/e0/Matadi%2C_Congo%2C_pedra_de_Ielala%2C_Diogo_C%C3%A3o.jpg/250px-Matadi%2C_Congo%2C_pedra_de_Ielala%2C_Diogo_C%C3%A3o.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Matadi,_Congo,_pedra_de_Ielala,_Diogo_C%C3%A3o.jpg)

Stone of Yellala, with the inscriptions of Diogo Cão

That Cão, on his second voyage of 1484–1486, was accompanied by [Martin Behaim](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Behaim "Martin Behaim") (as alleged on the latter's Nuremberg globe of 1492) is very doubtful. But it is known that the explorer revisited the Congo and erected two more _padrões_ on land beyond his previous voyage. The first was at Cabo Negro, Angola, the second at [Cape Cross](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cape_Cross "Cape Cross"). The Cape Cross pillar probably marked the end of his progress southward, some 1,400 kilometers.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diogo_C%C3%A3o#cite_note-EB1911-9) Diogo Cão also embarked the four indigenous ambassadors, that he had promised not to keep for more than fifteen moons.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diogo_C%C3%A3o#cite_note-Aderinto_2017_p._300-10)

Cão sailed 170 kilometers up the [Congo River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Congo_River "Congo River") to the [Yellala Falls](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yellala_Falls "Yellala Falls"). On the cliffs above this site an inscription was engraved which records the passage of Cão and his men: "Here arrived the ships of the illustrious monarch, [Dom João the Second of Portugal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_II_of_Portugal "John II of Portugal") – Diogo Cão, Pedro Anes, Pedro da Costa, Alvaro Pires, Pero Escolar".[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diogo_C%C3%A3o#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWinius199597-11)

### Death

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Diogo_C%C3%A3o&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Death")]

Information regarding Cão's death is scanty and contradictory. A legend on the [globe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Erdapfel "Erdapfel") created by Martin Behaim reads "_hic moritur_" (here he dies), seeming to indicate that the explorer lost his life on the coast of Africa in 1486 during his second voyage. However, sixteenth-century historian [João de Barros](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jo%C3%A3o_de_Barros "João de Barros") never mentions Cão's death but wrote instead of his return to the Congo, and subsequent taking of a native envoy back to Portugal.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diogo_C%C3%A3o#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWinius2003-12)

A report by a board of astronomers and pilots presented at a 1525 conference in Badajo clearly stated that his death happened near Serra Parda. A coast map by [Henricus Martellus Germanus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henricus_Martellus_Germanus "Henricus Martellus Germanus") published in 1489 indicated the location of a padrão erected by Diogo Cão in Ponta dos Farilhões nearby Serra Parda, with the legend "et hic moritur" ("and here he died").[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diogo_C%C3%A3o#cite_note-FOOTNOTERavenstein1900637-13)

## Padrões

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Diogo_C%C3%A3o&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Padrões")]

The four pillars set up by Cão on his two voyages have all been discovered still on their original site, and the inscriptions on two of them from Cape Santa Maria and Cape Cross, dated 1482 and 1485 respectively, are still to be read and have been printed. The Cape Cross padrão was long in Berlin (replaced on the spot by a granite facsimile) but was recently returned to Namibia; those from the Kongo estuary and the more southerly Cape Santa Maria and Cabo Negro are in the Museum of the Lisbon Geographical Society.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diogo_C%C3%A3o#cite_note-EB1911-9)

## Tributes post-mortem

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Diogo_C%C3%A3o&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Tributes post-mortem")]

In 1951, botanists named a genus of plants from western central tropical Africa in his honour, _[Diogoa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diogoa "Diogoa")_.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diogo_C%C3%A3o#cite_note-14)[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diogo_C%C3%A3o#cite_note-15)

In [Vila Real](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vila_Real "Vila Real"), the plaza Diogo Cão was named after him. In the center of the plaza, stands a bronze statue of him supported on a square granite pedestal base.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diogo_C%C3%A3o#cite_note-16)

In 1999, André Roubertou from the French Hydrographic Office (SHOM) named an undersea hole located off the southern coast of Portugal ([Gulf of Cádiz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gulf_of_C%C3%A1diz "Gulf of Cádiz")) the Diogo Cão Hole.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diogo_C%C3%A3o#cite_note-17)

In 2018, a [hopper dredger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trailing_suction_hopper_dredger "Trailing suction hopper dredger") called the Diogo Cao and immatriculated in Luxembourg was launched afloat.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diogo_C%C3%A3o#cite_note-18)

## In literature

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Diogo_C%C3%A3o&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: In literature")]

Diogo Cão is the subject of _Padrão_, one of the best-known poems in [Fernando Pessoa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fernando_Pessoa "Fernando Pessoa")'s book _[Mensagem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mensagem "Mensagem")_, the only one published during the author's lifetime.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diogo_C%C3%A3o#cite_note-19) He also figures strongly in the 1996 novel _Lord of the Kongo_ by Peter Forbath.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diogo_C%C3%A3o#cite_note-20)

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

Portuguese explorer (1452–1486)

For the Portuguese Navy frigate NRP _Diogo Cão_ (F 333), see [USS Formoe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/USS_Formoe "USS Formoe").
